title: My AI Assisted Game just left early access and its popping off.
author: Shalke97
selftext:
Grim Reach Idle started as a "let's see if this even works" project. I wanted a dark-fantasy idle RPG that felt like a real game rather than a spreadsheet: three combat styles that actually play differently, a slayer tower with contracts, dungeons, enchanting, a little settlement you build up, and a world that keeps working while you don't. I built the first version for myself, then handed it to a few friends to test. The Feedback was very very positive. That was the moment I decided to put it on Steam.

It went into Early Access first, while I kept working on it in the open, i didn't know when my game would be in a "complete" state. Six weeks of patches later it hit 1.0 (Mind you, i worked on it every day for around 8-10 Hours-ish), and a few days ago i shipped the first big post-launch update. 



How it was built 

I'm a solo dev (software developer IRL), but I haven't worked alone. Claude runs the studio side: think of it as the CEO and lead engineer in one seat. It plans the update, spawns specialised agents (content, engine, UI, balance, QA) that work in parallel on separate parts of the repo, verifies every delivery itself, and comes back to me only with decisions that are actually mine to make: is this the button style, does this drop rate feel right, do we ship.

Codex is the design agent. While the code side was being built, it generated the art in parallel from written briefs: monster and item art with real alpha, portraits for 60 playable archetypes, painted backdrops, UI mockups and more. It also writes its own QA notes and hands the assets over in a staging folder; nothing goes into the game before it's checked and signed off by me, of course.

My job is to be the one with taste and the one who says no. I test every build, I write the feedback that becomes the next patch, I decide what the game is. Honestly, the biggest lesson was that "AI assisted" only works if someone verifies everything. Every feature has a test, every UI change has a screenshot, every save from launch day still loads. The agents are fast; being right is still my responsibility.



Working with the community

This is the part I didn't expect to enjoy this much. Steam reviews and Discord reports turned into concrete patch notes within days: cooking that yields portions instead of single bites, dropped gear that finally beats crafted gear, an item wiki you can actually navigate, dungeons you can queue like everything else, and a slayer system that got a full second pass because people told me the tasks were too easy and the shop wasn't worth it. Several patch notes literally have a review number next to them. 



The game



Grim Reach Idle on Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4915450](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4915450)



Dark fantasy, idle progression, seven languages, offline progress, no microtransactions, saves that stay compatible across every update. If you try it, the feedback channels are the Steam forums and the in-game report button.



Happy to answer questions about the workflow, the agent setup, the verification pipeline, or the art side. It's been a strange, wonderful few months.

comments.author: Feline_Fan
comments.body: As a gamedev who does everything manually (no AI, just my time so no tokens to consider), what is the cost of a project like yours.  How many tokens/money does it costs to make?

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
Hey! Thanks for asking.  
I'm using Claude Max, which costs 180 Euros a month in addition to a higher GPT Tier which is around 120 Euros a month. So total cost each month is around 300 Euros and it produces everything i need. I noticed that Codex with a solid workflow can generate much better assets than using the on-site chatGPT. I wish i'd knew sooner, in the beginning i created around 800 Images in the web ChatGPT and Chroma Keyed everything myself. But i'm working on replacing alot of not-so-good looking assets with newer ones over time.

replies.author: Astra_Origin
replies.body: ChatGPT can generate images with transparent backgrounds since a week or so ago.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
https://preview.redd.it/olyc4l73uvlh1.png?width=3429&format=png&auto=webp&s=914195fa2bfc4cafc9b5f1ec7a53c5275b1c6a4b

But it wasn’t very reliable for me. I used to batch-generate ten images at a time, which was extremely tedious through the chat interface. Sometimes it would merge all ten individual images into one large collage or generate strange backgrounds with a fake PNG checkerboard pattern instead of actual transparency.

With my current workflow, however, every image is automatically checked for logic, art style, consistency, and a proper alpha channel. The entire process is now fully automated.

As you can see in the image, I’m currently working on a new character-creation system featuring different races, classes, and professions. Players will still be able to upload their own character images as well.

Compared with my older generations, however, the improvement in quality is immediately noticeable: sharp, clean lines, no chroma-key artifacts, and far more consistent results. It simply looks much better.

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body:
Before launching in Early Access, I spent around four weeks building the framework and another week working purely on the assets. Overall, it took roughly six or seven weeks before I released it on Steam. I chose Early Access because, at the time, I wasn’t sure how close the game was to being truly finished.

After about a month, I decided that I no longer wanted to sell it as an Early Access title. By then, it had grown into a complete game with 21 playable chapters, 20 skills, and plenty of endgame content.

I’m still expanding it, of course, and I’ll continue doing so as long as the revenue covers my AI-related costs. If those costs eventually outweigh the profit, I’ll have to stop. I genuinely love working on it, it’s fun, and creating a game like this has always been a dream of mine.. but i simply can’t afford to pay for everything every month without seeing any return. The first Month was an investment that turned out to be good. 

And I really appreciate the kind words!

comments.author: Shalke97
comments.body:
So, here’s the long post about my workflow!

I didn’t use anything pre-made. I built everything myself from scratch.

It all started with a project folder that acts as the central place for development. The first thing I did was create a Game Design Document with Claude. I think this is the part you should spend the most time on. Not only do you need to know exactly where you want the project to go, but the AI needs to understand it too. If I remember correctly, the prompt for my GDD was around two pages long in Microsoft Word.

After that, I created the structure for our little “game development studio.” I made one agent the CEO and studio lead, basically my second in command. Then we created several worker agents and gave all of them their own rules and responsibilities. There were game designers, debuggers, system testers and player agents for balancing.

The player agents had different player profiles, goals and ways of playing the game. They were a huge help with balancing because the testing agent created a separate gameplay flow for every type of player. This allowed it to give feedback on every step of the game from several different perspectives.

Once all of that was set up, we decided on the framework. From that point on, I handed the first few hours of development over to Claude, our CEO. I gave it permission to manage up to ten subagents at the same time. Their job was to build a playable alpha that we could use as the foundation for the game.

Of course, the first version wasn’t great, but it was good enough to build on. Every agent followed its own rules, and the CEO checked everything the other “employees” produced. If it found a problem, it immediately sent the work back to the responsible agent. Most of the time, I didn’t even see the broken version. By the time something reached me, it had already been reviewed and improved by the agents themselves.

That was basically my whole workflow with Claude. I check the results and give it clearly defined goals.

There really isn’t any magic behind it. When I read a lot of posts here, I sometimes feel like people overcomplicate the whole process with complicated harnesses, Git repositories and all kinds of additional systems. I personally found it more interesting to build my own workflow from scratch, and it worked very well for me.

Some people will probably say, “Of course that works for a 2D game,” and they’re not wrong. I’ve also started 3D projects that required a lot more attention. I still used the same general workflow for those projects, though, and it worked well there too. It just took longer.

Now for the game assets.

At the beginning, I generated everything through the ChatGPT website with a chroma key background and removed the background manually. The results weren’t always perfect, but they were good enough for what I needed at the time, especially since the game was still just a hobby project.

After creating around 800 to 900 images, I decided to upgrade my €20 ChatGPT subscription to the plan that costs roughly €120. I also wanted to use Codex because I sometimes reached the limits of my €180 Claude subscription.

After experimenting with it for a while and rethinking the workflow, Codex became the artist of our little studio.

I let Codex inspect my project, and Claude, acting as the CEO, wrote an explanation of what the project was, how it worked and what Codex’s role would be. Codex then created a simple template that Claude could fill out whenever a new asset was needed. Codex uses that information to generate assets that match the style of my game.

I feel like image generation through Codex CLI works differently from generation in the normal ChatGPT interface. At least the results feel different to me.

Codex also checks its own work. It has clear rules for alpha channels, transparent backgrounds, image dimensions, the art style and many other things related to the world and logic of my game. If an image doesn’t follow those rules, the main Codex agent notices it and generates the asset again until the result is correct.

This is probably the slowest part of the entire process, but it runs automatically. Right now, it has been generating 60 game assets for me for about an hour. These are male and female orcs covering 30 different classes, with 15 combat classes and 15 professions. I’ve already done the same thing for humans and elves.

Codex generates the whole batch, creates the folder on its own and saves everything in the correct place. Once it’s finished, it writes a text file with instructions for Claude. It’s basically a message saying, “I’m done. Here’s where you can find everything.”

That’s currently the only manual part of the process. I have to give that message to Claude myself. The message contains the path to the folder, so Claude knows where to find the assets and can add them to the game.

That’s the general workflow. I obviously can’t explain every small detail here because the post would become far too long, but I hope this gives you a decent idea of how I do it.

Maybe it will encourage some people to simply try building their own workflow instead of relying completely on tools made by someone else.

If you have any questions, feel free to ask.
